record.paper_title: Modeling social resilience: Questions, answers, open problems
record.original_question: How can data needed for social-resilience modeling be obtained from repositories of social organizations? The question should include extracting fine-grained interaction records from repositories such as git, constructing bipartite and projected collaboration networks, and deriving additional information about productivity or hierarchy.

evidence.quote: Questions • How can we obtain such data from repositories of social organizations?
These contain ﬁne-grained records of all changes made to the software, together with information who changed it, what was changed and when.
We developed a software package, git2net, that is able to extract this information, to create bipartite networks and their projections into an interaction network between developers
analyzing the amount of code changes can quantify the productivity of developers and analyzing the sequence of code changes gives insights into their hierarchical structure.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider a social organization whose collaborative activity is recorded in a version-control repository (e.g., a git repository) that logs, for every change, the developer who made the change, the file(s) and code regions affected, and a timestamp. Formalize and solve the following modeling problem:

(a) Define an extraction procedure that maps the raw commit history to a time-stamped bipartite interaction record B = {(d_i, f_i, t_i, Δ_i)}, where d_i is a developer, f_i is a file (or finer code unit), t_i is a time, and Δ_i quantifies the magnitude/type of the change (e.g., number of lines added/edited, edit-distance based weights).

(b) From B, construct (i) the bipartite developer–artifact network G_B = (D ∪ F, E_B) with weighted edges encoding aggregated contributions, and (ii) its one-mode projection G_D = (D, E_D) onto developers, specifying a co-editing rule (e.g., two developers are linked when they edit overlapping code regions within a temporal window τ) and a weighting scheme on E_D.

(c) Derive from B and G_D quantitative proxies for (i) individual and collective productivity (e.g., functionals of the contribution weights Δ_i over time) and (ii) hierarchy among developers (e.g., orderings inferred from the temporal sequence of edits to shared code, such as who edits whose code).

Question: Provide such an extraction-and-construction framework, prove that the resulting networks and derived measures are well-defined (independent of irrelevant repository artifacts such as merge commits or whitespace edits), and characterize their statistical properties (degree distributions, temporal motifs, hierarchy indices) for collaborative-software repositories.
artifact.status_search_result: A software tool (git2net) and associated methodology exist for extracting fine-grained co-editing interactions from git repositories and constructing bipartite and projected developer networks, and follow-up work uses these to study productivity and hierarchy. The general modeling question of how to best derive social-resilience-relevant data from such repositories remains an ongoing research program rather than a closed mathematical problem.

status_evidence.title: git2net - Mining Time-Stamped Co-Editing Networks from Git Repositories
status_evidence.snippet: We present git2net, a python package that facilitates the extraction of fine-grained co-editing networks from git repositories.
status_evidence.claim: A method/tool exists that extracts fine-grained co-editing bipartite and projected networks from git repositories.

status_evidence.title: Modeling social resilience: Questions, answers, open problems
status_evidence.snippet: Open problems regarding obtaining data for social-resilience modeling from organizational repositories.
status_evidence.claim: The broader modeling question is presented as an open research problem.
